name: Hay's Green
lede: Hay's Green is a moderate, yellow-leaning green, one of six colors Robert Ridgway's 1912 dictionary names for a person called only Hay, and its closest color-graph match is another of the six, Ackermann's Green.

sections.title: One of six colors named Hay's
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 “Color Standards and Color Nomenclature” lists Hay's Green at hex #5C825D among the names he credits to a person [1]. It shares its possessive with five other colors in the same book, among them [[hay-s-brown|Hay's Brown]], [[hay-s-maroon|Hay's Maroon]] and [[hay-s-russet|Hay's Russet]], but Ridgway never names the Hay he means, so the connection is undocumented in our sources [1]. The 1955 Inter-Society Color Council catalog repeats the name in the block it calls moderate yellowish green [1].

Its nearest neighbor in our color graph is [[dark-sage|Dark Sage]], only 2.8 units away and more vivid [1]. Closer still, within 3.4 units, sits [[ackermann-s-green|Ackermann's Green]], another name from Ridgway's same person-named group [1]. Against the basic color words it reads closest to [[viridian|Viridian]], 8.0 units off [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive matches this green in 0.59% of 23,781 paintings, 141 of them, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 65 [2]. That makes it more common than 53% of the named colors in our set [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 1.6% of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 5.1 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 26% of its 65 appearances [2]. Gustav Klimt is its most devoted painter here, holding it in 6 of 50 works, 10.2 times the baseline of the museums those paintings come from, and the color is also over-represented in Austria, 7.7 times the expected rate [2]. Our earliest match dates to 1445, by Dieric Bouts, 467 years before Ridgway's 1912 book recorded the name, a floor rather than a first, since a color match in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment [2].
